The report finishes. No snapshot can see 20.00 now, so VACUUM removes that version, and its space can be reused.

Page 12 with rows P3, P9 and P7, beside an undo log. Chips marked R and Q show which version a long report and a later query read.

A long report takes its snapshot while P7 costs 20.00. Then transaction 812 changes P7 to 22.00 and commits, and a new query starts.
PostgreSQL: the update adds a second version of P7, 22.00, to page 12 and marks the 20.00 version as replaced. The report keeps reading the 20.00 version on the page; the new query reads 22.00. When the report finishes, VACUUM removes the old version.
InnoDB: the update copies 20.00 into an undo record, then changes the row on page 12 to 22.00, with a pointer to the undo record. The new query reads 22.00 on the page; the report follows the pointer and rebuilds 20.00. When the report finishes, purge discards the undo record.

Four layers, top to bottom: WAL buffers, the operating system page cache, the drive’s write cache and its flash cells.

The commit record for transaction 812 sits in PostgreSQL’s WAL buffers.
PostgreSQL hands it to the operating system, which keeps it in its page cache. That is still memory.
fdatasync asks the operating system to send it to the drive. It lands in the drive’s write cache first.
This drive copies the cached data to its flash cells before it reports success.
fdatasync returns, and PostgreSQL replies COMMIT.
The power fails. Every volatile layer is wiped, but the commit record is in flash.
Recovery finds the commit record and replays the change. P7 costs 22.00.

PostgreSQL	A 24-byte header and a 4-byte line pointer, with padding to an 8-byte boundary. A null bitmap once any column is NULL.	8 kB
InnoDB	A 5-byte header, plus a list of variable-length field sizes and NULL flags. Every clustered-index record also holds a 6-byte transaction ID and a 7-byte roll pointer to its undo, and a 6-byte row ID when the table has no primary key.	16 kB
SQL Server	A 4-byte header, a null bitmap of 2 bytes plus a bit per column, 2 bytes plus 2 more for each variable-length column, and a 2-byte slot. Up to 14 bytes more once row versioning is in use.	8 kB, 8,096 bytes of it for rows

Engine	When a value moves out of the row	What stays behind

FIGURE 6

Page visits as the range widens

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id <= 79;

With the rows scattered, one customer matched (3 rows) means an index scan visits 3 pages and a sequential scan reads all 6. By the third customer, 8 rows or 22% of the table, the matches already sit on all six pages. With every row matched, an index scan makes 36 page visits, a bitmap heap scan still reads all 6 pages, and the sequential scan reads 6 pages in order without touching the index. With the same rows stored in customer order, the matches fill one page before reaching the next: 22 rows, 61% of the table, sit on 4 pages, and they reach all six only at 32 rows, 89%. The 60,000-order table is closer to the second order, because neighbouring rows have neighbouring customer numbers. There PostgreSQL chose a bitmap heap scan up to customer_id 500, reading 922 of the 1,725 pages, and a sequential scan from 550. On a copy with the rows shuffled, the same bitmap scan read all 1,715 of the copy’s pages.

FIGURE 10

The same keys, inserted in order and at random

-- top: order_id 1, 2, 3 … 75 (an auto-increment key)
-- bottom: the same 75 values, shuffled (like random UUIDs)

Two indexes receive the same 75 keys. Keys in order always go at the end: each page fills to 15 of its 16 slots, then the next key starts a new page, so the keys end on 5 pages, each 15/16 full. Keys in random order land on whichever page covers their value. When that page is full it splits, and half its entries move to a new page beside it. After six splits the same keys take 7 pages, each between 8 and 15 of 16 slots full. On the 60,000-order table, PostgreSQL’s primary key took 166 pages with the keys inserted in order and about 225 with the same keys inserted at random.

FIGURE 6

Page visits as the range widens

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id <= 79;

With the rows scattered, one customer matched (3 rows) means an index scan visits 3 pages and a sequential scan reads all 6. By the third customer, 8 rows or 22% of the table, the matches already sit on all six pages. With every row matched, an index scan makes 36 page visits, a bitmap heap scan still reads all 6 pages, and the sequential scan reads 6 pages in order without touching the index. With the same rows stored in customer order, the matches fill one page before reaching the next: 22 rows, 61% of the table, sit on 4 pages, and they reach all six only at 32 rows, 89%. The 60,000-order table is closer to the second order, because neighbouring rows have neighbouring customer numbers. There PostgreSQL chose a bitmap heap scan up to customer_id 500, reading 922 of the 1,725 pages, and a sequential scan from 550. On a copy with the rows shuffled, the same bitmap scan read all 1,715 of the copy’s pages.
